metadata.title: Weighted local Weyl laws for elliptic operators

extraction_notes.note: Section 3.1 heuristics are proof sketches of Theorems 1.1/1.2 (proved in full later): kept as proof nodes with alternative proves edges; the sketch rule asks rigor semi_formal but rigor is not allowed on proofs, so no rigor was set.

Appendix A is a section-long proof of Theorem 2.2 (one proof node, subsections as steps); its notation-introducing sentences are kept as Level-1 definitions nested in the steps because the appendix lemmas use them.
Numbered claims are claim environments with separate prf environments; environment spans were kept (claim node plus separate proof node) instead of step rule 7's claim-spans-its-argument.
The opening of Section 6 starts the argument for Theorem 2.5 in prose before Lemmas 6.1-6.2; extracted as definitions of Q_1, I_L, II_L and equation (27) rather than as a first proof part.
Remark 7 asserts and justifies two families of admissible symbols (could be two claims); kept as one remark since it is used as a whole by the proof of Theorem 1.2.
prf environments not adjacent to their lemma (a remark or a sentence intervenes); proves edges to Lemma 4.3 and Lemma 5.1 inferred from content.
The proof of Claim 4 opens with 'Let us prove the following formula' and the whole proof establishes it; nesting would give a single top step, so steps were kept flat.
Figure 1 (the proof dependency map announced at the end of Section 3) is omitted from the source; dependencies were taken from the text only.
Acknowledgements, section road-maps and forward pointers ('We prove Theorem X in Section Y') are not nodes; informal summaries of corollaries before their statements were not extracted.

nodes.name: Closed manifold X with density
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a smooth compact manifold without boundary, of positive dimension $n>0$ and equipped with a smooth positive density $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$.

nodes.name: Positive elliptic differential operator A of order m
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a positive elliptic differential operator on $\mathcal{X}$ of positive order $m$.

nodes.name: Ellipticity of a differential operator in coordinates
nodes.statement_short: In local coordinates $A=\sum a_\alpha\partial^\alpha$ and its top-order symbol $\sigma_A(x,\xi)=\sum_{|\alpha|=m}a_\alpha\xi^\alpha$ is positive off $\xi=0$.
nodes.statement: By this we mean that in any local coordinate system $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ on $\mathcal{X}$ defined on $U\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, $A$, acts on $C^\infty_c(U)$ as \[ \sum_{0\leq |\alpha|\leq m} a_{\alpha}(x)\partial^\alpha \] where $\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^n$ and $a_\alpha\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and for each $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}$, we have \[ \sigma_A(x,\xi):=\sum_{|\alpha|=m}a_\alpha(x)\xi^\alpha>0\, .

nodes.name: Principal symbol
nodes.statement: The function $\sigma_A$ is called the \textbf{principal symbol} of $A$ in these coordinates.

nodes.name: Principal symbol is a function on T*X minus zero section
conclusions: the principal symbol of $A$ read in different coordinates pieces together as a smooth function on the complement of the zero section in $T^*\mathcal{X}$
nodes.statement: It is well known (and easy to check) that the principal symbol of $A$ read in different coordinates pieces together as a smooth function on the complement of the zero section in $T^*\mathcal{X}$.

nodes.name: A symmetric
nodes.statement: We assume that $A$ is symmetric with respect to the $L^2$-scalar product on $(\mathcal{X},d\mu_{\mathcal{X}})$.

nodes.name: Discrete spectrum and eigenbasis of A
nodes.statement_short: $A$ has a unique self-adjoint extension with eigenvalues $\lambda_k\to+\infty$ and smooth orthonormal eigenfunctions $e_k$ forming a Hilbert basis.
conclusions: $A$ has a unique self-adjoint extension whose spectrum is made up of a non-decreasing sequence $(\lambda_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ of positive eigenvalues diverging to $+\infty$
nodes.statement: Then one can show (see Subsection \ref{ss.setting}) that $A$ has a unique self-adjoint extension whose spectrum is made up of a non-decreasing sequence $(\lambda_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ of positive eigenvalues diverging to $+\infty$ with smooth $L^2$-normalized eigenfunctions $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ forming a Hilbert basis for $L^2(\mathcal{X},d\mu_{\mathcal{X}})$.

nodes.name: Spectral projector Pi_L
nodes.statement: For each $L\geq 0$, let $\Pi_L$ be the $L^2$ orthogonal projector on the space spanned by the eigenfunctions $e_k$ such that $\lambda_k\leq L$.

nodes.name: Spectral function E_L
nodes.statement_short: $E_L(x,y)=\sum_{\lambda_k\le L}e_k(x)\overline{e_k(y)}$, the smooth kernel of $\Pi_L$.
nodes.statement: Since this space is finite-dimensional, $\Pi_L$ has a smooth integral kernel $E_L\in C^\infty(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X})$. More explicitely, \[ \forall (x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X},\, E_L(x,y)=\sum_{\lambda_k\leq L}e_k(x)\overline{e_k(y)}\, .

nodes.name: Weyl's law
nodes.statement_short: The eigenvalue counting function grows like $(2\pi)^{-n}\mathrm{vol}\{\sigma_A\le1\}\,L^{n/m}$.
conclusions: \textup{Card}\{k\in\mathbb{N}\ |\ \lambda_k\leq L\}\sim
nodes.statement: Integrating $E_L$ over the diagonal he recovered the following estimate, also known as \textbf{Weyl's law}: \[ \textup{Card}\{k\in\mathbb{N}\ |\ \lambda_k\leq L\}\sim \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\mathcal{X}}\int_{\sigma_A(x,\xi)\leq 1}\widetilde{d_x\mu_{\mathcal{X}}}(\xi) d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}(x)\times L^{\frac{n}{m}} \] where $\widetilde{d_x\mu_{\mathcal{X}}}(\xi)$ is the density induced on $T^*_x\mathcal{X}$ by $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$.

nodes.name: Weighted spectral kernel K_L^s
nodes.statement_short: $K_L^s(x,y)=\sum_{\lambda_k\le L}\lambda_k^{-s}e_k(x)\overline{e_k(y)}$.
nodes.statement: For each $s\in\mathbb{R}$ we consider the kernel \[ K_L^s(x,y)=\sum_{\lambda_k\leq L} \lambda_k^{-s} e_k(x)\overline{e_k(y)}\, .

nodes.name: Meromorphic continuation of the diagonal kernel of A^{-s}
conclusions: as a function of $s$, the limit admitted a meromorphic extension to the whole complex plane
nodes.statement: In \cite{sch86}, the author proved that, as a function of $s$, the limit admitted a meromorphic extension to the whole complex plane.

nodes.name: Weighted local Weyl laws
nodes.statement: We call these results \textbf{weighted local Weyl laws} by analogy with $E_L$ (which is just $K_L^0$) because of the weights $\lambda_n^{-s}$ on the terms of the sum defining $K^s_L$.

nodes.name: Weighted local Weyl law for s<n/m (differential operators)
nodes.statement_short: For $s<n/m$, derivatives of $K^s_L$ rescaled at scale $L^{-1/m}$ converge to the Fourier transform of $\mathbb{1}[\sigma_A\le1]\sigma_A^{-s}$, with error $O(L^{-1/m}\ln L^\eta)$; off-diagonal they are smaller.
assumptions: $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$ agrees with the Lebesgue measure in these coordinates
conclusions: there exists $V\subset U$ an open neighborhood of $0$ such that, in these coordinates, we have the following estimates
nodes.statement: Assume that $s<\frac{n}{m}$. Fix $x_0\in\mathcal{X}$ and consider local coordinates $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ for $\mathcal{X}$ centered at $x_0$ and defined on an open subset $U\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$ agrees with the Lebesgue measure in these coordinates. Then for each $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{N}^n$, there exists $V\subset U$ an open neighborhood of $0$ such that, in these coordinates, we have the following estimates. \begin{enumerate} \item Uniformly for $w,x,y\in V$ and $L\geq 1$ we have $w+L^{-1/m}x, w+L^{-1/m}y\in U$ and \begin{align*} L^{s-(n+|\alpha|+|\beta|)/m}\partial^\alpha_x\partial^\beta_yK^s_L\left(w+L^{-1/m}x,w+L^{-1/m}y\right)=&\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma_A(w,\xi)\leq 1}e^{i\langle \xi,x-y\rangle}\frac{(i\xi)^\alpha(-i\xi)^\beta}{\sigma_A(w,\xi)^s} d\xi\\ &+O\left(L^{-1/m}\ln\left(L\right)^\eta\right) \end{align*} where $\eta = 1$ if $s=(n+|\alpha|+|\beta|-1)/m$ and $0$ otherwise. \item Let $\varepsilon>0$. Then, uniformly for $x,y\in V$ such that $|x-y|>\varepsilon$ and $L\geq 1$, \[ L^{s-(n+|\alpha|+|\beta|)/m}\partial^\alpha_x\partial^\beta_y K^s_L(x,y)=O\left(L^{-1/m}\ln\left(L\right)^\eta\right) \] where $\eta = 1$ if $s=(n+|\alpha|+|\beta|-1)/m$ and $0$ otherwise. \end{enumerate} Here $|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\dots+\alpha_n$ and $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the Euclidean scalar product.
nodes.label: t.diff.1

nodes.name: Hörmander's theorem as the case s=0
nodes.statement: Note that the case where $s=0$ and $\alpha=\beta=0$ is Theorem 5.1 of \cite{ho68} (see Theorem \ref{t.hormander} and the discussion below for more details about this case).

nodes.name: Canonical dual density on T*X
nodes.statement_short: The density on $T^*\mathcal{X}$ that is Lebesgue in coordinates where $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$ is Lebesgue.
nodes.statement: Firstly, $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$ defines a canonical dual density $\widetilde{d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}}$ on $T^*\mathcal{X}$. Around any $x\in\mathcal{X}$, there exist local coordinates in which $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$ corresponds to the Lebesgue measure.

nodes.name: Unit cosphere S*_x of the symbol
nodes.statement: For each $x\in\mathcal{X}$, let $S^*_x=\{\xi\in T^*_x\mathcal{X}\, |\, \sigma_A(x,\xi)=1\}$.

nodes.name: Density d_x nu on S*_x (polar decomposition)
nodes.statement_short: $S^*_x$ is a star-shaped hypersurface carrying a density $d_x\nu$ such that Lebesgue measure on $T^*_x$ decomposes in polar form $d_x\nu\,t^{n-1}dt$.
nodes.statement: Since $\sigma_A$ is $m$-homogeneous, $S^*_x$ is a smooth compact hypersurface of $T^*_x\mathcal{X}$ strictly star-shaped\footnote{More precisely, for each $\xi\in T^*_x\mathcal{X}\setminus\{0\}$, the ray $\{t\xi\, |\, t>0\}$ intersects $S^*$ exactly at $\sigma_A(x,\xi)^{-1/m}\xi$ and does so transversally.} around the origin and there exists a smooth density $d_x\nu$ on $S^*_x$ such that for each $u\in C^\infty_c(T^*_x\mathcal{X})$, \begin{equation} \int_{T^*_x\mathcal{X}} u(\xi)\widetilde{d_x\mu_{\mathcal{X}}}(\xi)=\int_0^{+\infty}\int_{S^*_x} u(t\xi) d_x\nu(\xi) t^{n-1}dt\, . \end{equation}

nodes.name: Polar decomposition of the cotangent density
nodes.statement: \int_{T^*_x\mathcal{X}} u(\xi)\widetilde{d_x\mu_{\mathcal{X}}}(\xi)=\int_0^{+\infty}\int_{S^*_x} u(t\xi) d_x\nu(\xi) t^{n-1}dt\, .
nodes.label: e.nu

nodes.name: Weighted local Weyl law for s=n/m (differential operators)
nodes.statement_short: For $s=n/m$, derivatives of $K^s_L$ still have rescaled limits, but $K^s_L$ itself behaves like $g_A[\ln L^{1/m}-\ln_+(L^{1/m}|x-y|)]+O(1)$: a logarithmic singularity smoothed at scale $L^{-1/m}$.
assumptions: $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$ agrees with the Lebesgue measure in these coordinates
conclusions: there exists an open neighborhood $V\subset U$ of $0$ such that the following holds

nodes.name: Theorem 3 of [ale161] (Laplacian on surfaces, s=1)
nodes.statement_short: The log-singular asymptotic of the second point of Theorem 1.2 for the Laplacian on a closed surface with s=1.
assumptions: $s=1$, $\mathcal{X}$ was a closed surface (so $n=2$) with a Riemmanian metric and $A$ was the associated Laplacian (so $m=2$)
conclusions: which proved the second point
nodes.statement: This theorem (especially the second point) generalizes Theorem 3 of \cite{ale161}, which proved the second point in the case where $s=1$, $\mathcal{X}$ was a closed surface (so $n=2$) with a Riemmanian metric and $A$ was the associated Laplacian (so $m=2$).

nodes.name: Log-singularity of the kernel of A^{-n/m}
nodes.statement_short: The kernel of $A^{-n/m}$ is integrable and equals $-g_A\ln d(x,y)$ plus a bounded symmetric function smooth off the diagonal.
assumptions: for each smooth distance function $d:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ on $\mathcal{X}$
conclusions: The Schwartz kernel $K\in\mathcal{D}'(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X})$ of $A^{-n/m}$ belongs to $L^1(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X})$.
there exists a bounded symmetric function $Q_{A,d}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$, smooth on the complement of the diagonal
nodes.statement: The Schwartz kernel $K\in\mathcal{D}'(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X})$ of $A^{-n/m}$ belongs to $L^1(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X})$. Moreover, for each smooth distance function $d:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ on $\mathcal{X}$ there exists a bounded symmetric function $Q_{A,d}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$, smooth on the complement of the diagonal, such that, for any distinct $x,y\in\mathcal{X}$, \[ K(x,y)=-g_A(x,y)\ln\left(d\left(x,y\right)\right)+Q_{A,d}(x,y)\, . \]
nodes.label: co.diff.1

nodes.name: Closed Riemannian manifold (X,g)
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathcal{X},g)$ be a closed Riemmanian manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$.

nodes.name: Laplacian and Riemannian volume density
nodes.statement: Let $\Delta=-div\circ\nabla$ be the Laplace operator on $\mathcal{X}$ and let $|dV_g|$ be the Riemmanian volume density on $\mathcal{X}$.

nodes.name: Principal symbol of the Laplacian
conclusions: $\Delta$ is an elliptic differential operator with principal symbol $\sigma(x,\xi)=g_x^{-1}\left(\xi,\xi\right)$
nodes.statement: Then, $\Delta$ is an elliptic differential operator with principal symbol $\sigma(x,\xi)=g_x^{-1}\left(\xi,\xi\right)$ where $g^{-1}_x$ is the scalar product induced on $T^*_x\mathcal{X}$ by $g_x$.

nodes.name: Laplacian is symmetric
conclusions: $\Delta$ is symmetric with respect to the $L^2$-scalar product induced by the density $|dV_g|$ on $\mathcal{X}$
nodes.statement: Moreover, $\Delta$ is symmetric with respect to the $L^2$-scalar product induced by the density $|dV_g|$ on $\mathcal{X}$.

nodes.name: Laplace eigenvalues
nodes.statement: Let $\left(\lambda_k\right)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ be the sequence of eigenvalues of $\Delta$ (counted with multiplicity) and arranged in increasing order.

nodes.name: Real Laplace eigenbasis
nodes.statement: Let $\left(e_k\right)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a Hilbert basis of $L^2\left(\mathcal{X},|dV_g|\right)$ made up of real valued functions, such that for each $k\in\mathbb{N}$, $\Delta e_k=\lambda_k e_k$.

nodes.name: Truncated Laplacian kernel K^s_L
nodes.statement: For each $L>0$, each $s>0$ and each $(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}$, let \[ K^s_L(x,y)=\sum_{0<\lambda_k\leq L}\lambda_k^{-1}e_k(x)e_k(y)\, . \]

nodes.name: K^1_L converges to the Green function (GFF covariance)
conclusions: $K^1_L$ converges in distribution as $L\rightarrow+\infty$ to the Green function on $\mathcal{X}$
nodes.statement: Then, $K^1_L$ converges in distribution as $L\rightarrow+\infty$ to the Green function on $\mathcal{X}$ which is the (generalized) covariance function for the Gaussian Free Field (see for instance \cite{shef_gff}).

nodes.name: Weighted local Weyl law for the Laplacian, s<n/2
nodes.statement_short: For the Laplacian and $s<n/2$, rescaled derivatives of $K^s_L$ converge to $(2\pi)^{-n}\int_{|\xi|_w\le1}e^{i\langle\xi,x-y\rangle}(i\xi)^\alpha(-i\xi)^\beta|\xi|_w^{-2s}d\xi$ times $L^{(n+|\alpha|+|\beta|-2s)/2}$.
assumptions: $|dV_g|$ agrees with the Lebesgue measure in these coordinates
conclusions: for each $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{N}^n$ there exists $V\subset U$ an open neighborhood of $0$ such that, in these coordinates, we have the following estimates
nodes.statement: Assume that $s<n/2$. Fix $x_0\in\mathcal{X}$ and consider local coordinates $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ for $\mathcal{X}$ centered at $x_0$ such that $|dV_g|$ agrees with the Lebesgue measure in these coordinates. Then, for each $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{N}^n$ there exists $V\subset U$ an open neighborhood of $0$ such that, in these coordinates, we have the following estimates. \begin{enumerate} \item Uniformly for $w,x,y\in V$ and $L\geq 1$ we have $w+L^{-1/2}x,w+L^{-1/2}y\in U$ and \begin{multline*} \partial_x^\alpha\partial_y^\beta K^s_L\left(w+L^{-1/2}x,w+L^{-1/2}y\right)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{|\xi|_w^2\leq 1}e^{i\langle\xi,x-y\rangle}\frac{(i\xi)^\alpha(-i\xi)^\beta}{|\xi|_w^{2s}} d\xi L^{(n+|\alpha|+|\beta|-2s)/2}\\ +O\left(L^{(n+|\alpha|+|\beta|-2s-1)/2}\ln\left(L\right)^\eta\right) \end{multline*} where $\eta=1$ if $s=(n+|\alpha|+|\beta|-1)/2$ and $0$ otherwise. Here $|\xi|_w^2=g^{-1}_w(\xi,\xi)$ and $d\xi$ is the Lebesgue measure. \item Let $\varepsilon>0$. Then, uniformly for $x,y\in V$ such that $|x-y|>\varepsilon$ and for $L\geq 1$, \[ \partial_x^\alpha\partial_y^\beta K^s_L\left(w+L^{-1/2}x,w+L^{-1/2}y\right)=O\left(L^{(n+|\alpha|+|\beta|-2s-1)/2}\ln\left(L\right)^\eta\right) \] where $\eta=1$ if $s=(n+|\alpha|+|\beta|-1)/2$ and $0$ otherwise. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: c.gff.1

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.4
nodes.statement_short: Specialize Theorem 1.1 to $A=\Delta$, $m=2$.
nodes.statement: This follows directly from Theorem \ref{t.diff.1} with $m=2$, $s<n/2$, $A=\Delta$ and $\sigma_A(w,\xi)=|\xi|_w^2$.

nodes.name: Corollary 1.5 recovers Theorem 3 of [ale161]
nodes.statement: Note that when $s=1$, the first part of the second point of Corollary \ref{c.gff.2} below yields Theorem 3 of \cite{ale161}.

nodes.name: Weighted local Weyl law for the Laplacian, s=n/2 (Gaussian free field)
nodes.statement_short: For the Laplacian and $s=n/2$, derivatives have rescaled limits and the kernel is $\frac{|S^{n-1}|}{(2\pi)^n}[\ln L^{1/2}-\ln_+(L^{1/2}|x-y|)]+O(1)$.
assumptions: $|dV_g|$ agrees with the Lebesgue measure in these coordinates
conclusions: there exists an open neighborhood $V\subset U$ of $0$ such that the following holds
nodes.statement: Assume that $s=n/2$. Fix $x_0\in\mathcal{X}$ and consider local coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2)$ for $\mathcal{X}$ centered at $x_0$ defined on an open subset $U\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ such that $|dV_g|$ agrees with the Lebesgue measure in these coordinates. Then, for each $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{N}^2$, there exists an open neighborhood $V\subset U$ of $0$ such that the following holds. \begin{enumerate} \item \begin{itemize} \item Assume that $(\alpha,\beta)\neq(0,0)$. In these coordinates, uniformly for $w,x,y\in V$ and $L\geq 1$, we have $w+L^{-1/2}x,w+L^{-1/2}y\in U$ and \begin{multline*} \partial^\alpha_x\partial^\beta_yK^s_L\left(w+L^{-1/2}x,w+L^{-1/2}y\right)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{|\xi|_w^2\leq 1} e^{i\langle\xi,x-y\rangle}\frac{(i\xi)^\alpha(-i\xi)^\beta}{|\xi|_w^n}d\xi L^{(n+|\alpha|+|\beta|-2s)/2}\\ +O\left(L^{(n+|\alpha|+|\beta|-2s-1)/2}\ln(L)^\eta\right) \end{multline*} where $\eta=1$ if $1=|\alpha|+|\beta|$ and $0$ otherwise. Here $|\xi|_w^2=g_w^{-1}(\xi,\xi)$ and $d\xi$ is the Lebesgue measure. \item Let $\varepsilon>0$. Then, uniformly for $x,y\in V$ such that $|x-y|>\varepsilon$ and for $L\geq 1$, \[ \partial_x^\alpha\partial_y^\beta K^s_L\left(w+L^{-1/2}x,w+L^{-1/2}y\right)=O\left(L^{(n+|\alpha|+|\beta|-2s-1)/2}\ln\left(L\right)^\eta\right) \] where $\eta=1$ if $1=|\alpha|+|\beta|$ and $0$ otherwise. \end{itemize} \item \begin{itemize} \item Uniformly for $x,y\in V$ and $L\geq 1$, in these coordinates, \[ G_L(x,y)=\frac{\left|S^{n-1}\right|}{(2\pi)^n}\left[\ln\left(L^{1/2}\right)-\ln_+\left(L^{1/2}|x-y|\right)\right]+O(1) \] where $\ln_+(t)=\ln(t)\vee 0$. \item There exists a symmetric bounded function $Q:U\times U\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ such that, uniformly for $\kappa\geq 1$, $L\geq 1$ and $x,y\in V$ such that $|x-y|\geq \kappa L^{-1/2}$, in these coordinates, \[ G_L(x,y)=\frac{\left|S^{n-1}\right|}{(2\pi)^n}\ln(|x-y|)+Q(x,y)+O\left(\kappa^{-1/2}\right)\, . \] \end{itemize} \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: c.gff.2

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.5
nodes.statement_short: Specialize Theorem 1.2 to $A=\Delta$, $m=2$, $s=n/2$.
nodes.statement: This follows directly from Theorem \ref{t.diff.2} with $m=2$, $s=n/2$, $A=\Delta$ and $\sigma_A(w,\xi)=|\xi|_w^2$.

nodes.name: Setting 1: closed manifold
nodes.statement: Here $\mathcal{X}$ is a compact manifold without boundary.

nodes.name: Setting 1: classical elliptic pseudo-differential operator A
nodes.statement: We consider a classical elliptic pseudo-differential operator $A$ of positive order $m$ acting on $C^\infty_c(\mathcal{X})$.

nodes.name: Setting 1: A symmetric
nodes.statement: We assume $A$ is symmetric for the $L^2$-scalar product on $(\mathcal{X},d\mu_{\mathcal{X}})$.

nodes.name: Principal symbol real and positive homogeneous
assumptions: We assume $A$ is symmetric for the $L^2$-scalar product on $(\mathcal{X},d\mu_{\mathcal{X}})$.
conclusions: the principal symbol $\sigma_A$ of $A$ is real valued and positive homogeneous of order $m$
nodes.statement: This implies that the principal symbol $\sigma_A$ of $A$ is real valued and positive homogeneous of order $m$.

nodes.name: Discrete spectrum in Setting 1
conclusions: $A$ has a unique self-adjoint extension in $L^2(\mathcal{X},d\mu_{\mathcal{X}})$ whose spectrum forms a discrete non-decreasing sequence $(\lambda_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ of real numbers diverging to $+\infty$
nodes.statement: Moreover, under these assumptions, $A$ has a unique self-adjoint extension in $L^2(\mathcal{X},d\mu_{\mathcal{X}})$ whose spectrum forms a discrete non-decreasing sequence $(\lambda_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ of real numbers diverging to $+\infty$ and whose corresponding eigenfunctions $e_k$ are of class $C^\infty$ (see for instance Section 29.1 of \cite{ho_apdo4}).

nodes.name: Spectral function E_L (general setting)
also_stated_at: For each $L>0$, set \[ \forall x,y\in\overline{\mathcal{X}}, E_L(x,y)=\sum_{\lambda_j\leq L}e_j(x)\overline{e_j(y)}\, . \]
nodes.statement: For each $L>0$, set \[ \forall x,y\in\overline{\mathcal{X}}, E_L(x,y)=\sum_{\lambda_j\leq L}e_j(x)\overline{e_j(y)}\, . \]

nodes.name: Setting 2: manifold with boundary
nodes.statement: Here $\mathcal{X}$ is the interior of a compact manifold $\overline{\mathcal{X}}$ with non-empty boundary $\partial\mathcal{X}$.

nodes.name: Setting 2: positive density
nodes.statement: We assume that $\mathcal{X}$ is equipped with a positive density $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$.

nodes.name: Dirichlet eigenvalue problem
nodes.statement_short: Find $\lambda$ and $u$ with $Au=\lambda u$ in $\mathcal{X}$ and $B_ju=0$ on $\partial\mathcal{X}$, for $A$ elliptic of even order.
nodes.statement: We consider the Dirichlet eigenvalue problem \begin{align*} Au&=\lambda u\text{ on }\mathcal{X}\, ;\\ \forall j=1,\dots,j_0,\, B_ju&=0\text{ on }\partial\mathcal{X} \end{align*} where $A$ is an elliptic differential operator of even order $m\geq 1$ with principal symbol $\sigma_A$, $B_j$ are boundary differential operators (see Chapter 2, Section 1.4 of \cite{lions_magenes_1}) and $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$.

nodes.name: Setting 2: elliptic, self-adjoint, semi-bounded problem
nodes.statement: We assume that the problem is elliptic, formally self-adjoint with respect to $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$ and semi-bounded from below (see \cite{vas83} Section 1).

nodes.name: Discrete spectrum of the Dirichlet problem
conclusions: the values of $\lambda$ for which this problem has a non-trivial solution with sufficient regularity form an non-decreasing sequence $(\lambda_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ of real numbers diverging to $+\infty$
nodes.statement: As is well known, under these assumptions, the values of $\lambda$ for which this problem has a non-trivial solution with sufficient regularity form an non-decreasing sequence $(\lambda_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ of real numbers diverging to $+\infty$ and the corresponding eigenfunctions $e_k$ are smooth in $\mathcal{X}$ up to the boundary (the proof goes along the same lines as in the closed case treated in Section 29.1 of \cite{ho_apdo4} and is easily adapted using results from Chapter 20 of \cite{ho_apdo3}).

nodes.name: Proper phase function
differentia: The function $\psi$ is a symbol of order one in its third variable.
nodes.statement_short: A symbol of order one vanishing where $\langle x-y,\xi\rangle=0$, with $\partial_x\psi|_{y=x}=\xi$, asymptotically 1-homogeneous in $\xi$.
nodes.statement: Given an open subset $U\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, we will say that a function $\psi\in C^\infty(U\times U\times\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a \textbf{proper phase function} if it satisfies the following conditions. \begin{enumerate} \item The function $\psi$ is a symbol of order one in its third variable. \item For each $(x,y,\xi)\in U\times U\times\mathbb{R}^n$, $\langle x-y,\xi\rangle =0$ implies that $\psi(x,y,\xi)=0$. \item For each $x\in U$ and $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n$, $\partial_x\psi(x,y,\xi)|_{y=x}=\xi$. \item There exists $\psi_\infty\in C^\infty(U\times U\times \mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\})$ satisfying all of the above properties and $1$-homogeneous in $\xi$ such that \[t^{-1}\psi(x,y,t\xi)\xrightarrow[t\to+\infty]{}\psi_\infty(x,y,\xi)\] where the convergence takes place in $S^1(U\times U\times \mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\})$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: d.phase

nodes.name: Linear phase <x-y,xi>
nodes.statement: An important example of proper phase function to have in mind is the phase function $\psi(x,y,\xi)=\langle x-y,\xi\rangle$.

nodes.name: Hörmander's local Weyl law
nodes.statement_short: Near the diagonal, $PE_L$ equals $(2\pi)^{-n}\int_{\sigma_A\le L}e^{i\psi}\sigma_P(\partial_{x,y}\psi)d\xi$ up to $O(L^{(n+d-1)/m})$, with $\psi$ a proper phase solving the eikonal equation.
assumptions: Let $P$ be a differential operator of order $d$ acting on $C^\infty(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X})$.
Suppose further that the density $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$ agrees with the Lebesgue measure in these coordinates.
conclusions: there exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $0\in\mathbb{R}^n$, a proper phase function function $\psi\in C^\infty(U\times U\times\mathbb{R}^n)$ and a constant $C<+\infty$
for each neighborhood $W\subset U\times U$ of the diagonal there exists $C>0$
there exists a symbol $\sigma\in S^1$ such that $\sigma_A^{1/m}-\sigma\in S^0$
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a differential operator of order $d$ acting on $C^\infty(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X})$. Fix a point in $\mathcal{X}$ and consider local coordinates $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ around it. Suppose further that the density $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$ agrees with the Lebesgue measure in these coordinates. Let $\sigma_A$ (resp. $\sigma_P$) be the principal symbol of $A$ (resp. $P$) in these coordinates. Then, there exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $0\in\mathbb{R}^n$, a proper phase function function $\psi\in C^\infty(U\times U\times\mathbb{R}^n)$ and a constant $C<+\infty$, such that, in these coordinates, for each $x,y\in U$ and $L>0$, \[ \left|PE_L(x,y)-\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma_A(x,\xi)\leq L}e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}\sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}\psi(x,y,\xi))d\xi\right|\leq C(1+L)^{(n+d-1)/m}\, . \] Moreover, for each neighborhood $W\subset U\times U$ of the diagonal there exists $C>0$ such that in local coordinates, for each $(x,y)\in \left(U\times U\right)\setminus W$ and $L>0$, \[ \Big|PE_L(x,y)\Big|\leq C(1+L)^{(n+d-1)/m}\, . \] Finally, there exists a symbol $\sigma\in S^1$ such that $\sigma_A^{1/m}-\sigma\in S^0$ and for each $x,y\in U$ and $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n$, \begin{equation} \sigma(x,\partial_x\psi(x,y,\xi))=\sigma(y,\xi)\, . \end{equation}
nodes.label: t.hormander

nodes.name: Eikonal equation
nodes.statement: \sigma(x,\partial_x\psi(x,y,\xi))=\sigma(y,\xi)\, .
nodes.label: e.eikonal

nodes.name: Notation d_{x,y} psi
nodes.statement: Here $\partial_{x,y}\psi$ denotes the partial derivative of $\psi$ with respect to the couple $(x,y)$.

nodes.name: Coordinate dependence of the asymptotic
nodes.statement: The asymptotic provided by Theorem \ref{t.main.2} is coordinate dependent since the notion of proper phase function is not invariant.

nodes.name: Eikonal equation
nodes.statement: Equation \eqref{e.eikonal} is called the \textbf{eikonal equation} and it has a unique solution with the boundary conditions imposed by the admissibility condition (see Section 3 of \cite{ho68}). The part concerning the eikonal equation is not usually stated as part of the local Weyl law but the function $\psi$ provided by the theorem does satisfy this property and it will be useful in our proofs.

nodes.name: History of the local Weyl law for general P
nodes.statement: The case where $P=Id$ and was proved by H\"ormander in \cite{ho68}. The case where $x=y$ and $\mathcal{X}$ is a closed manifold was treated in \cite{sava_adep} with some restrictions on $P$. Finally, Gayet and Welschinger extended this result to a general $P$ (see Theorem 2.3 of \cite{gawe14}) on a closed manifold. While in their statement, $x=y$, their proof yields the off-diagonal case with only minor modifications.

nodes.name: Compactness assumption
nodes.statement: H\"ormander manages to lift the compactness assumption using results on the local nature of the spectral projector $\Pi_L$. It is not clear that this approach could be applied for a general $P$.

nodes.name: Only interior estimates in the boundary case
nodes.statement: Notice that in the boundary problem case (as in setting 2. form Subsection \ref{ss.setting}) we only get estimates in the interior of the domain.

nodes.name: Canzani-Hanin monochromatic projector
nodes.statement: One recent result closely related to this theorem is Canzani and Hanin's asymptotics for the monochromatic spectral projector of the Laplacian under some dynamical assumption on the geodesic flow (see \cite{caha151} and \cite{caha16}).

nodes.name: Weighted local Weyl law, subcritical case n+d+m Re z>0
nodes.statement_short: For $f(t)=t^z$ with $n+d+m\,\mathrm{Re}\,z>0$, $PK_L$ rescaled at scale $L^{-1/m}$ near the diagonal matches the Fourier integral of $\sigma_A^z\sigma_P$ over $\{\sigma_A\le1\}$ up to $O(L^{-1/m}\ln L^\eta)$.
assumptions: Let $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ such that $f(t)=t^z$ for $t$ large enough.
conclusions: there exists an open neighborhood $V$ of $0\in U$ such that the following holds
nodes.statement: Fix $z=z_1+iz_2\in\mathbb{C}$. Let $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ such that $f(t)=t^z$ for $t$ large enough. Let $K_L$ be the Schwartz kernel of $\Pi_Lf(A)$. Suppose that $n+d+mz_1>0$. For each $x,y\in U$ and $L\geq 1$, let \[R_L(x,y)=L^{-z_1-(n+d)/m}\Big[PK_L(x,y)-\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma_A(0,\xi)\leq 1}e^{i\langle \xi,x-y\rangle L^{1/m}}\sigma_A(0,\xi)^z\sigma_P(0,0,(\xi,-\xi))d\xi\Big].\] Then, there exists an open neighborhood $V$ of $0\in U$ such that the following holds. \begin{enumerate} \item Uniformly for $L\geq 1$ and $(w,x,y)\in V\times V\times V$, $w+L^{-1/m}x, w+L^{-1/m}y\in U$ and \[ R_L\left(w+L^{-1/m}x,w+L^{-1/m}y\right)=O\left(L^{-1/m}\ln(L)^\eta\right) \] where $\eta=1$ if $n+d+mz=1$ and $0$ otherwise. \item Uniformly for $L\geq 1$ and $(x,y)\in V\times V\setminus W$, \[ PK_L(x,y)=O\left(L^{z_1+(n+d-1)/m}\ln(L)^\eta\right) \] where $\eta=1$ if $n+d+mz=1$ and $0$ otherwise. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: t.main.1

nodes.name: k_0-admissible symbol
nodes.statement_short: At every point some derivative of order $k\le k_0$ of $\sigma$ differs from that of the power of a linear form, i.e. $\sigma^{k-1}\partial^k_\xi\sigma\ne c_{m,k}(\partial_\xi\sigma)^{\otimes k}$.
nodes.statement: Fix $m\in\mathbb{R}$, $m>0$ and $k_0\in\mathbb{N}$, $k_0\geq 2$. We say that a positive $m$-homogeneous symbol $\sigma$ on $U$ is $k_0$-admissible there exists $k_0\geq 2$ such that \begin{equation} \forall (x,\xi)\in U\times(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus \{0\})\ \exists k\in\{2,\dots,k_0\},\ \sigma(x,\xi)^{k-1}\partial_\xi^k\sigma(x,\xi)\neq \frac{m(m-1)\dots(m-k+1)}{m^k}(\partial_\xi\sigma(x,\xi))^{\otimes k}. \end{equation}
nodes.label: d.admissible

nodes.name: Admissibility condition
nodes.statement: \forall (x,\xi)\in U\times(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus \{0\})\ \exists k\in\{2,\dots,k_0\},\ \sigma(x,\xi)^{k-1}\partial_\xi^k\sigma(x,\xi)\neq \frac{m(m-1)\dots(m-k+1)}{m^k}(\partial_\xi\sigma(x,\xi))^{\otimes k}.
nodes.label: e.admissible

nodes.name: Coordinate invariance of admissibility
nodes.statement: This condition is invariant if we see $\sigma$ as a function on $T^*\mathcal{X}$ because coordinate changes act linearly on the fibers of $T^*\mathcal{X}$.

nodes.name: Weighted local Weyl law, critical case n+d+mz=0 (logarithmic)
nodes.statement_short: When $n+d+mz=0$ and $\sigma_A$ is admissible (or $n=1$), $PK_L\approx(2\pi)^{-n}Y_P[\ln L^{1/m}-\ln_+(L^{1/m}|x-y|)]$, and away from scale $L^{-1/m}$ it is $-(2\pi)^{-n}Y_P\ln|x-y|+Q$.
assumptions: Suppose that $n+d+mz=0$ and that either $n=1$ or $\sigma_A$ is a $k_0$-admissible symbol for some $k_0\geq 2$.
conclusions: there exists $V\subset U$ an open neighborhood of $0$ such that the following holds
nodes.statement: We use the same notations as in Theorem \ref{t.main.1}. Suppose that $n+d+mz=0$ and that either $n=1$ or $\sigma_A$ is a $k_0$-admissible symbol for some $k_0\geq 2$. For each $x,y\in U$ let \[ Y_P(x,y)=\int_{S^*_y}\sigma_P\left(x,y,\partial_{x,y}(\partial_\xi\psi(x,y,0)\xi)\right)d_y\nu(\xi)\, . \] Then, there exists $V\subset U$ an open neighborhood of $0$ such that the following holds. \begin{enumerate} \item Uniformly for $(x,y)\in V\times V$ and $L\geq 1$, \[ PK_L(x,y)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}Y_P(x,y)\Big[\ln\left(L^{1/m}\right)-\ln_+\left(L^{1/m}|x-y|\right)\Big]+O(1)\, . \] \item There exists $Q\in L^\infty(V\times V)$ such that, uniformly for $\kappa\geq 1$, $L\geq 1$ and $(x,y)\in V\times V$ such that $|x-y|\geq \kappa L^{-1/m}$, \[ PK_L(x,y)=-\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}Y_P(x,y)\ln(|x-y|)+Q(x,y)+O\left(\kappa^{-1/k_0}\right)\, . \] Here, if $n=1$ we set $k_0=1$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: t.main.2

nodes.name: Examples of admissible symbols: strictly convex level sets and polynomial symbols
nodes.statement_short: Symbols with strictly convex level sets are 2-admissible and positive homogeneous polynomial symbols of degree m are m-admissible, so Theorem 2.5 applies to all differential operators.
nodes.statement: The admissibility condition on the symbol of $A$ may appear to be unfamiliar. However, in practice, it is often satisfied. Here are two important examples of families of admissible symbols: \begin{itemize} \item If $n\geq 2$ and the level sets $S^*_x$ are strictly convex, $\partial^2_\xi\sigma_A$ is positive when restricted to their tangent spaces. Therefore, it cannot be a multiple of $\left(\partial_\xi\sigma\right)^{\otimes 2}$ so Theorem \ref{t.main.2} applies with $k_0=2$. \item If $\sigma_A$ is a positive homogeneous polynomial of degree $m\in\mathbb{N}$ in $\xi$, $m\geq 1$, then it is $m$-admissible. Indeed, otherwise, taking $k=k_0=m$, we would have, for some $(x,\xi)\in U\times\left(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\right)$, $\sigma_A(x,\xi)^{m-1}\partial_\xi^m\sigma_A(x,\xi)=0$. But since $\sigma_A(x,\xi)>0$ we have $\partial_\xi^m\sigma_A(x,\xi)=0$ which implies that all the coefficients of $\sigma_A(x,\cdot)$ vanish. This contradicts the fact that $\sigma_A(x,\xi)>0$. In particular, Theorem \ref{t.main.2} applies for all differential operators. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: r.examples

nodes.name: Genericity of admissible symbols
nodes.statement_short: For $n\ge2$ there is $k_0(n)$ such that $k_0$-admissible symbols form an open dense set of positive $m$-homogeneous symbols in the Whitney topology.
assumptions: Fix $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $n\geq 2$ and let $U\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be an open subset.
conclusions: There exists $k_0=k_0(n)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for each $m>0$, the set of $k_0$-admissible symbols is open and dense in the set of positive $m$-homogeneous symbols on $U$
nodes.statement: Fix $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $n\geq 2$ and let $U\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be an open subset. There exists $k_0=k_0(n)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for each $m>0$, the set of $k_0$-admissible symbols is open and dense in the set of positive $m$-homogeneous symbols on $U$ for the topology induced by the Whitney topology through the restriction map to the (Euclidean) unit sphere bundle on $U$.
nodes.label: t.fat

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.6
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from Proposition 7.5.
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{t.fat} follows immediately from Proposition \ref{p.fat}, which is proved Subsection \ref{ss.whitney}.

nodes.name: Weighted kernel limit, supercritical case n+d+m Re z<0
nodes.statement_short: If $n+d+m\,\mathrm{Re}\,z<0$, $PK_L$ converges locally uniformly to $PK_\infty$ with $K_\infty\in C^d$, at rate $O(L^{z_1+(n+d)/m})$.
conclusions: there exists and a function $K_\infty\in C^d(U\times U)$ such that the following holds
nodes.statement: We use the same notations as in Theorem \ref{t.main.1}. Suppose that $n+d+mz_1<0$. Then, there exists and a function $K_\infty\in C^d(U\times U)$ such that the following holds. For each compact subset $\Omega\subset U\times U$, uniformly for $(x,y)\in \Omega$, \[ PK_L(x,y)=PK_\infty(x,y)+O\left(L^{z_1+(n+d)/m}\right)\, . \]
nodes.label: t.main.3

nodes.name: Setting enters only through Hörmander's theorem
nodes.statement: In Theorems \ref{t.main.1}, \ref{t.main.2} and \ref{t.main.3}, the setting provided in Subection \ref{ss.setting} only comes into play through Theorem \ref{t.hormander}. Therefore, if one could weaken the hypotheses for this theorem, one would automatically extend Theorems \ref{t.main.1} and \ref{t.main.2} as a corollary. In particular, since H\"ormander proves Theorem \ref{t.hormander} for $P=Id$ without any compactness assumption or boundary condition, both of these results remain valid in this case.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 2.3 with $z=-s$ and $P=\partial^\alpha_x\partial^\beta_y$.
nodes.statement: Both results follow from Theorem \ref{t.main.1} applied to the first setting of Subsection \ref{ss.setting} with $z=-s$ by taking $P=\partial^\alpha_x\partial^\beta_y$ in a neighborhood of $0$. In this case, the order of $P$ is $d=|\alpha|+|\beta|$ and we have \[ \sigma_P(x,y,\xi)=(i\xi)^\alpha(-i\xi)^\beta \] for any $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and $x,y\in V$ close enough to $0$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement_short: First part from Theorem 2.3 with $P=\partial^\alpha_x\partial^\beta_y$; second part from Theorem 2.5 with $P=Id$, using $m$-admissibility of differential symbols and symmetry of $K^s_L$.

nodes.name: First part via Theorem 2.3
nodes.statement_short: Set $z=-n/m$ and $P=\partial^\alpha_x\partial^\beta_y$; since $(\alpha,\beta)\ne0$, $n+d+mz_1>0$ and Theorem 2.3 applies.
nodes.statement: Set $z=-s=-n/m$. For the first part, set $P=\partial^\alpha_x\partial^\beta_y$ near $0$ and proceed as in the proof of Theorem \ref{t.diff.1}. Indeed, since $(\alpha,\beta)\neq (0,0)$, we have $n+d+mz_1=|\alpha|+|\beta|>0$.

nodes.name: Second part via Theorem 2.5
nodes.statement_short: Differential symbols are $m$-admissible, so Theorem 2.5 with $P=Id$ gives $Y_P=\nu_y(S^*_y)$.
nodes.statement: For the second part, since by Remark \ref{r.examples} $\sigma_A$ is $m$-admissible, and since $n+d+mz_1=0$, we apply Theorem \ref{t.main.2} instead. In our case, $P=Id$ so for each $x,y\in U$, $Y_P(x,y)=\nu_y\left(S^*_y\right)$ so \[ K^s_L(x,y)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\nu_y\left(S^*_y\right)\left[\ln\left(L^{1/m}\right)-\ln_+\left(L^{1/m}|x-y|\right)\right]+O(1)\, . \]

nodes.name: Symmetrize
nodes.statement_short: Hermitian symmetry lets one replace $\nu_y(S^*_y)$ by its average with $\nu_x(S^*_x)$.
nodes.statement:
But since $K^s_L(x,y)=\overline{K^s_L(y,x)}$, we may replace $
u_y\left(S^*_yight)$ in the above expression by $ rac{
u_x\left(S^*_xight)+
u_y\left(S^*_yight)}{2}$. as announced.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.3
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the limit $L\to\infty$ in Theorem 1.2 by dominated convergence, change $\ln|x-y|$ to $\ln d(x,y)$, and use pseudo-differential regularity for smoothness off the diagonal.
nodes.statement: We use the notations of Theorem \ref{t.main.2}. First of all, by definition, as $L\rightarrow +\infty$, $K_L^s\rightarrow K$ in distribution. Moreover, by Theorem \ref{t.diff.2}, any point in $\mathcal{X}$ has a neighborhood $V$ such that the sequence $(K_L^s)_{L\geq 1}$ is uniformly bounded on $V\times V$ by a locally integrable function and converge pointwise towards $-g_A(x,y)\ln\left(|x-y|\right)+Q(x,y)$ where $Q\in L^\infty(V\times V)$ on the complement of the diagonal in $V\times V$. In particular, they converge in distribution to this function. This implies that when restricted to $C^\infty(V\times V)$, \[ K(x,y)=-g_A(x,y)\ln\left(|x-y|\right)+Q(x,y)\, . \] Now, given any smooth distance $d$ on $\mathcal{X}$, for each $x,y$ distinct, \[ \ln\left(|x-y|\right)=\ln\left(d(x,y)\right)+\ln\left(\frac{|x-y|}{d(x,y)}\right) \] and the second term is bounded so, on $V\times V$, \[ K(x,y)=-g_A(x,y)\ln\left(d(x,y)\right)+Q_A(x,y) \] for some $Q_A\in L^\infty(V\times V)$. But $K$ is the integral kernel of $A^s$ which is a self-adjoint pseudo-differential operator (see \cite{see67} or Proposition 29.1.9 of \cite{ho_apdo4}). In particular, it is smooth and symmetric outside the diagonal (see for instance Theorem 18.1.16 of \cite{ho_apdo3}). Hence, $Q_A$ must also be symmetric and smooth outside the diagonal.

nodes.name: Distributional limit
nodes.statement_short: $K^s_L\to K$ in distribution.
nodes.statement: We use the notations of Theorem \ref{t.main.2}. First of all, by definition, as $L\rightarrow +\infty$, $K_L^s\rightarrow K$ in distribution.

nodes.name: Local identification of K
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1.2 gives a locally integrable dominating bound and pointwise limit, so $K=-g_A\ln|x-y|+Q$ locally.
nodes.statement: Moreover, by Theorem \ref{t.diff.2}, any point in $\mathcal{X}$ has a neighborhood $V$ such that the sequence $(K_L^s)_{L\geq 1}$ is uniformly bounded on $V\times V$ by a locally integrable function and converge pointwise towards $-g_A(x,y)\ln\left(|x-y|\right)+Q(x,y)$ where $Q\in L^\infty(V\times V)$ on the complement of the diagonal in $V\times V$. In particular, they converge in distribution to this function. This implies that when restricted to $C^\infty(V\times V)$, \[ K(x,y)=-g_A(x,y)\ln\left(|x-y|\right)+Q(x,y)\, . \]

nodes.name: Change of distance
nodes.statement_short: $\ln|x-y|-\ln d(x,y)$ is bounded, so the formula holds with $d$.
nodes.statement: Now, given any smooth distance $d$ on $\mathcal{X}$, for each $x,y$ distinct, \[ \ln\left(|x-y|\right)=\ln\left(d(x,y)\right)+\ln\left(\frac{|x-y|}{d(x,y)}\right) \] and the second term is bounded so, on $V\times V$, \[ K(x,y)=-g_A(x,y)\ln\left(d(x,y)\right)+Q_A(x,y) \] for some $Q_A\in L^\infty(V\times V)$.

nodes.name: Symmetry and smoothness of Q
nodes.statement_short: $A^s$ is a self-adjoint pseudo-differential operator, so its kernel is smooth and symmetric off the diagonal.
nodes.statement: But $K$ is the integral kernel of $A^s$ which is a self-adjoint pseudo-differential operator (see \cite{see67} or Proposition 29.1.9 of \cite{ho_apdo4}). In particular, it is smooth and symmetric outside the diagonal (see for instance Theorem 18.1.16 of \cite{ho_apdo3}). Hence, $Q_A$ must also be symmetric and smooth outside the diagonal.

nodes.name: Introduction results also hold in Setting 2
nodes.statement: These proofs work also in Setting 2 of Subsection \ref{ss.setting} instead of that of Setting 1, so all of the results from the introduction hold also in Setting 2.

nodes.name: Heuristic derivation of Theorem 1.1 for the Laplacian
nodes.statement_short: Heuristic sketch for the Laplacian: write $K^s_L$ as a Stieltjes integral of $E_\lambda$, insert Hörmander's asymptotic with $\psi\approx\langle x-y,\xi\rangle$, use polar coordinates and rescale.
nodes.statement: In order to get a sense of the kind of calculations we will carry out in the rest of the article, let us present a simple example, with few non-rigorous steps in order to shorten the argument. We assume that $\mathcal{X}$ is a closed Riemmanian manifold and that $A$ denotes the associated Laplacian\footnote{Here we use the convention that $\Delta = -\textup{div}\circ\nabla$ so that the operator is positive.}. Then, $A$ is indeed elliptic of order $m=2$ and self-adjoint with respect to the riemmanian volume density $d\mu$. Moreover the symbol of $A$ is $\sigma_A(x,\xi) = \|\xi\|_x^2$ where $\|\cdot\|_x$ is the norm induced by the riemmanian metric on $T^*_x\mathcal{X}$. Thus, in orthonormal coordinates $S^*_x = S^{n-1}$. Finally, we take $P=Id$. Now, if $s\geq \frac{n}{2}$, \begin{equation} K^s_L(x,y)=\int_1^L \lambda^{-s} E_\lambda '(x,y)d\lambda + O(1)=s\int_1^L\lambda^{-s-1} E_\lambda(x,y)d\lambda+O(1)\, . \end{equation} Here, we artificially cut-off the first eigenvalues since they contribute a constant term to the sum defining $K^s_L$. By Theorem \ref{t.hormander}, \begin{equation} E_L(x,y) \simeq \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{|\xi|^2\leq L} e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)} d\xi \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \psi(x,y,\xi)\simeq \langle x-y,\xi\rangle\, . \end{equation} Replacing $E_\lambda'$ in Equation \eqref{e.heuristic.1} the expression given by Equations \eqref{e.heuristic.2} and \eqref{e.heuristic.3} we get \[ K^s_L(x,y)\simeq \frac{s}{(2\pi)^{n/2}}\int_1^L \lambda^{-s-1}\int_{\|\xi\|^2\leq \lambda}e^{i\langle x-y,\xi\rangle} d\xi d\lambda\, . \] At this point, we make the additional assumption that $n\geq 2$. The one dimensional case is similar in spirit but follows a different argument. We then continue with a polar change of coordinates: $\xi=t\omega$. \begin{equation} K^s_L(x,y)\simeq \frac{s}{(2\pi)^n}\int_1^L\lambda^{-s-1} \int_0^{\lambda^{1/2}}J_{x,y}(t) t^{n-1}dt d\lambda \end{equation} where \[ J_{x,y}(t)=\int_{S^{n-1}} e^{it\langle x-y,\omega\rangle} d\omega\, . \] Let us first assume that $s>\frac{n}{2}$ and take $x-y = L^{-1/2}h$ where $h\in\mathbb{R}^n$ is fixed. Then, \begin{align*} K^s_L(x,y)&\simeq \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{S^{n-1}} \int_1^L \lambda^{-s} \int_0^{\lambda^{1/2}} e^{i L^{-1/2}t \langle h,\omega \rangle}t^{n-1} dt d\lambda d\omega\\ &\simeq \frac{s}{(2\pi)^n}L^{n/2-s}\int_{S^{n-1}}\int_0^1 \lambda^{-s-1} \int_0^{\lambda^{1/2}} e^{it \langle h,\omega \rangle}t^{n-1}dt d\lambda d\omega\\ &\simeq\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n} \int_{\|\xi\|^2\leq 1} \|\xi\|^{-s} e^{i\langle h,\xi\rangle} d\xi L^{n/2-s}\, . \end{align*} This is the conclusion of Theorem \ref{t.diff.1}.

nodes.name: Laplacian setting
nodes.statement_short: Take $A$ the Laplacian, $m=2$, $S^*_x=S^{n-1}$, $P=Id$.
nodes.statement: In order to get a sense of the kind of calculations we will carry out in the rest of the article, let us present a simple example, with few non-rigorous steps in order to shorten the argument. We assume that $\mathcal{X}$ is a closed Riemmanian manifold and that $A$ denotes the associated Laplacian\footnote{Here we use the convention that $\Delta = -\textup{div}\circ\nabla$ so that the operator is positive.}. Then, $A$ is indeed elliptic of order $m=2$ and self-adjoint with respect to the riemmanian volume density $d\mu$. Moreover the symbol of $A$ is $\sigma_A(x,\xi) = \|\xi\|_x^2$ where $\|\cdot\|_x$ is the norm induced by the riemmanian metric on $T^*_x\mathcal{X}$. Thus, in orthonormal coordinates $S^*_x = S^{n-1}$. Finally, we take $P=Id$.

nodes.name: Integration by parts in lambda
nodes.statement_short: Write $K^s_L$ as $s\int_1^L\lambda^{-s-1}E_\lambda d\lambda+O(1)$.
nodes.statement: Now, if $s\geq \frac{n}{2}$, \begin{equation} K^s_L(x,y)=\int_1^L \lambda^{-s} E_\lambda '(x,y)d\lambda + O(1)=s\int_1^L\lambda^{-s-1} E_\lambda(x,y)d\lambda+O(1)\, . \end{equation} Here, we artificially cut-off the first eigenvalues since they contribute a constant term to the sum defining $K^s_L$.

nodes.name: Insert Hörmander's asymptotic
nodes.statement_short: Replace $E_\lambda$ by the Fourier integral with phase $\approx\langle x-y,\xi\rangle$.
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{t.hormander}, \begin{equation} E_L(x,y) \simeq \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{|\xi|^2\leq L} e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)} d\xi \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \psi(x,y,\xi)\simeq \langle x-y,\xi\rangle\, . \end{equation} Replacing $E_\lambda'$ in Equation \eqref{e.heuristic.1} the expression given by Equations \eqref{e.heuristic.2} and \eqref{e.heuristic.3} we get \[ K^s_L(x,y)\simeq \frac{s}{(2\pi)^{n/2}}\int_1^L \lambda^{-s-1}\int_{\|\xi\|^2\leq \lambda}e^{i\langle x-y,\xi\rangle} d\xi d\lambda\, . \]

nodes.name: Polar coordinates
nodes.statement_short: Polar coordinates $\xi=t\omega$ introduce the spherical integral $J_{x,y}(t)$.
nodes.statement: At this point, we make the additional assumption that $n\geq 2$. The one dimensional case is similar in spirit but follows a different argument. We then continue with a polar change of coordinates: $\xi=t\omega$. \begin{equation} K^s_L(x,y)\simeq \frac{s}{(2\pi)^n}\int_1^L\lambda^{-s-1} \int_0^{\lambda^{1/2}}J_{x,y}(t) t^{n-1}dt d\lambda \end{equation} where \[ J_{x,y}(t)=\int_{S^{n-1}} e^{it\langle x-y,\omega\rangle} d\omega\, . \]

nodes.name: Rescaling at L^{-1/2}
nodes.statement_short: With $x-y=L^{-1/2}h$, rescaling gives the Fourier transform of $\|\xi\|^{-s}$ on the unit ball times $L^{n/2-s}$.
nodes.statement: Let us first assume that $s>\frac{n}{2}$ and take $x-y = L^{-1/2}h$ where $h\in\mathbb{R}^n$ is fixed. Then, \begin{align*} K^s_L(x,y)&\simeq \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{S^{n-1}} \int_1^L \lambda^{-s} \int_0^{\lambda^{1/2}} e^{i L^{-1/2}t \langle h,\omega \rangle}t^{n-1} dt d\lambda d\omega\\ &\simeq \frac{s}{(2\pi)^n}L^{n/2-s}\int_{S^{n-1}}\int_0^1 \lambda^{-s-1} \int_0^{\lambda^{1/2}} e^{it \langle h,\omega \rangle}t^{n-1}dt d\lambda d\omega\\ &\simeq\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n} \int_{\|\xi\|^2\leq 1} \|\xi\|^{-s} e^{i\langle h,\xi\rangle} d\xi L^{n/2-s}\, . \end{align*} This is the conclusion of Theorem \ref{t.diff.1}.

nodes.name: Heuristic: K^s_L as integral of E_lambda
nodes.statement: K^s_L(x,y)=\int_1^L \lambda^{-s} E_\lambda '(x,y)d\lambda + O(1)=s\int_1^L\lambda^{-s-1} E_\lambda(x,y)d\lambda+O(1)\, .
nodes.label: e.heuristic.1

nodes.name: Heuristic: Hörmander approximation of E_L
nodes.statement: E_L(x,y) \simeq \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{|\xi|^2\leq L} e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)} d\xi
nodes.label: e.heuristic.2

nodes.name: Heuristic: psi approximately linear
nodes.statement: \psi(x,y,\xi)\simeq \langle x-y,\xi\rangle\, .
nodes.label: e.heuristic.3

nodes.name: Heuristic: polar form of K^s_L
nodes.statement: K^s_L(x,y)\simeq \frac{s}{(2\pi)^n}\int_1^L\lambda^{-s-1} \int_0^{\lambda^{1/2}}J_{x,y}(t) t^{n-1}dt d\lambda
nodes.label: e.heuristic.4

nodes.name: Heuristic derivation of Theorem 1.2 for the Laplacian
nodes.statement_short: Heuristic sketch for $s=n/2$: stationary phase decay of $J_{x,y}$ lets one replace it by an indicator, giving a $\int du/u$ logarithm.
nodes.statement: Assume now that $s=\frac{n}{2}$. Starting off from Equation \eqref{e.heuristic.4}, we get \[ K_L^s(x,y)\simeq \frac{s}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{|x-y|^2}^{|x-y|^2L}\lambda^{-s-1}\int_0^{\lambda^{1/2}}J_{x,y}(|x-y|^{-1}t) t^{n-1}dt d\lambda\, . \] Note that, by the stationary phase method, \begin{equation} J_{x,y}(t) = O\left((|x-y|t)^{-1/2}\right)\, . \end{equation} This crucial observation basically allows us to replace $J_{x,y}(|x-y|^{-1}t)$ with $|S^{n-1}|\mathds{1}[|x-y|^{-1}t\leq 1]$ and get \begin{align*} K_L^s(x,y)&\simeq \frac{s|S^{n-1}|}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{|x-y|^2}^{|x-y|^2L}\lambda^{-s-1}\int_0^{\lambda^{1/2}}\mathds{1}[|x-y|^{-1}t\leq 1] t^{n-1}dtd\lambda\\ & = \dots\\ & = \frac{|S^{n-1}|}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{|x-y|}^{|x-y|L^{1/2}}\mathds{1}[u\leq 1]\frac{du}{u}+O(1)\\ & = \frac{|S^{n-1}|}{(2\pi)^n}\ln\left(L^{1/2}\right)-\ln_+\left(L^{1/2}|x-y|\right) + O(1)\, . \end{align*} This is the essential statement of Theorem \ref{t.diff.2}.

nodes.name: Rescale by |x-y|
nodes.statement_short: Change variables in the polar formula to scale by $|x-y|$.
nodes.statement: Assume now that $s=\frac{n}{2}$. Starting off from Equation \eqref{e.heuristic.4}, we get \[ K_L^s(x,y)\simeq \frac{s}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{|x-y|^2}^{|x-y|^2L}\lambda^{-s-1}\int_0^{\lambda^{1/2}}J_{x,y}(|x-y|^{-1}t) t^{n-1}dt d\lambda\, . \]

nodes.name: Stationary phase decay
nodes.statement_short: $J_{x,y}(t)=O((|x-y|t)^{-1/2})$, so $J$ can be replaced by $|S^{n-1}|\mathbb{1}[\cdot\le1]$.
nodes.statement: Note that, by the stationary phase method, \begin{equation} J_{x,y}(t) = O\left((|x-y|t)^{-1/2}\right)\, . \end{equation}

nodes.name: Logarithmic integral
nodes.statement_short: The resulting $\int du/u$ gives $\ln L^{1/2}-\ln_+(L^{1/2}|x-y|)$.
nodes.statement: This crucial observation basically allows us to replace $J_{x,y}(|x-y|^{-1}t)$ with $|S^{n-1}|\mathds{1}[|x-y|^{-1}t\leq 1]$ and get \begin{align*} K_L^s(x,y)&\simeq \frac{s|S^{n-1}|}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{|x-y|^2}^{|x-y|^2L}\lambda^{-s-1}\int_0^{\lambda^{1/2}}\mathds{1}[|x-y|^{-1}t\leq 1] t^{n-1}dtd\lambda\\ & = \dots\\ & = \frac{|S^{n-1}|}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{|x-y|}^{|x-y|L^{1/2}}\mathds{1}[u\leq 1]\frac{du}{u}+O(1)\\ & = \frac{|S^{n-1}|}{(2\pi)^n}\ln\left(L^{1/2}\right)-\ln_+\left(L^{1/2}|x-y|\right) + O(1)\, . \end{align*} This is the essential statement of Theorem \ref{t.diff.2}.

nodes.name: Heuristic: stationary phase decay of J
nodes.label: e.heuristic.5

nodes.name: Amplitude H_P and oscillatory integral J_A
nodes.statement_short: $H_P=e^{i\psi(x,y,t\xi)}\sigma_P(x,y,t^{-1}\partial_{x,y}\psi(x,y,t\xi))$ and $J_A(x,y,t)=\int_{S^*_y}H_P\,d_y\nu$.
nodes.statement: For any $t>0$, $x,y\in U$ and $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n$ let \begin{equation} H_P(x,y,\xi,t)=e^{i\psi(x,y,t\xi)}\sigma_P\left(x,y,t^{-1}\partial_{x,y}\psi(x,y,t\xi)\right) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} J_A(x,y,t)=\int_{S^*_y}H_P(x,y,\xi,t)d_y\nu(\xi). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of H_P
nodes.statement: H_P(x,y,\xi,t)=e^{i\psi(x,y,t\xi)}\sigma_P\left(x,y,t^{-1}\partial_{x,y}\psi(x,y,t\xi)\right)

nodes.name: Definition of J_A
nodes.statement: J_A(x,y,t)=\int_{S^*_y}H_P(x,y,\xi,t)d_y\nu(\xi).
nodes.label: e.osc

nodes.name: Scaling of H_P

nodes.statement_short: For $k_0$-admissible $\sigma_A$, $|J_A(x,y,t)|\le C(t|x-y|)^{-1/k_0}$ near $0$.
conclusions: there exists $V\subset U$ an open neighborhood of $0$ and $C<+\infty$ such that, uniformly for distinct $x,y\in V$ and $t>0$
nodes.statement: Assume that $\sigma_A$ is $k_0$-admissible. Then, there exists $V\subset U$ an open neighborhood of $0$ and $C<+\infty$ such that, uniformly for distinct $x,y\in V$ and $t>0$ \[ |J_A(x,y,t)|\leq C\left(t|x-y|\right)^{-\frac{1}{k_0}}\, . \]
