nodes.name: A.2 Estimating the convolved kernel
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotic of $\rho*\tilde E_{L,P}$ (Lemma A.3 via Lemmas A.4-A.6).
nodes.statement: In this section we provide the following expression for $\rho*\tilde{E}_{L,P}$ in the local coordinates chosen in Lemma \ref{l.source}. \begin{lemma} There is an open set $V\subset U$ containing $0$ such that, as $L\rightarrow\infty$ and uniformly for $(x,y)\in V\times V$, \[\rho*\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L} \sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}\psi(x,y,\xi)) e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi + O(L^{n+d-1})\,.\] \end{lemma} In order to do so we use the three lemmas stated below, whose proofs are given at the end of the section. To begin with, we use the information of Lemma \ref{l.source} to give a first expression for $\rho*\tilde{E}_{L,P}$. \begin{lemma} The quantity \[\rho*\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)-\int_{-\infty}^L\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{T^*_yM} \mathcal{F}^{-1}_t\Big[\mathcal{F}(\rho)P\left(q(x,t,y,\xi)e^{i(\psi(x,y,t,\xi)-t \sigma(y,\xi))}\right)\Big](\lambda)d\xi d\lambda\] is bounded uniformly for $(x,y)\in U\times U$. \end{lemma} Here and below $\mathcal{F}$ is the Fourier transform and the occasional subscript indicates the variable on which the transform is taken. Let us now investigate the effect of the differential operator $P$ on the right hand side of this expression. By the Leibniz rule, there is a finite family of symbols $(\sigma_j)_{0\leq j\leq d}\in C^{\infty}(U\times]-\varepsilon,\varepsilon[\times U,\mathbb{R}^n)^{d+1}$ such that for each $j$, $\sigma_j$ is homogeneous of degree $j$, such that \[P\Big[q(x,t,y,\xi)e^{i(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t\sigma(y,\xi))}\Big]=\Big[\sum_{j=0}^{d} \sigma_j(x,t,y,\xi)\Big]e^{i(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t\sigma(y,\xi))}\] and such that \[\sigma_d(x,t,y,\xi)=q(x,t,y,\xi)\sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t\sigma(y,\xi)))\,.\] Now, for each $j$, let \[R_j(x,y,L,\xi)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n+1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathcal{F}(\rho)(t)\sigma_j(x,t,y,\xi)e^{itL}dt\] and \[S_j(x,y,L)=\int_{-\infty}^L\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} R_j(x,y,\lambda-\sigma(y,\xi),\xi)e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi d\lambda\,.\] Then, \[\int_{-\infty}^L\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \mathcal{F}^{-1}_t\Big[\mathcal{F}(\rho)P\left(q(x,t,y,\xi)e^{i(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t \sigma(y,\xi))}\right)\Big](\lambda)d\xi d\lambda=\sum_{j=0}^dS_j(x,y,L)\,.\] Each $S_j$ will grow at an order corresponding to the degree of the associated symbol. This is shown in the following lemma. \begin{lemma} There is an open set $V\subset U$ containing $0$ such that, as $L\rightarrow\infty$ and uniformly for $(x,y)\in V\times V$, \[S_j(x,y,L)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L}\sigma_j(x,0,y,\xi)e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi+O(L^{n+j-1})\,.\] \end{lemma} Similarly since $q(x,0,y,\xi)-1\in S^{-1}(U_0\times U_0,\mathbb{R}^n)$, from a computation analogous to the proof of Lemma \ref{hol3} and left to the reader, replacing $\sigma_d$ by \[(q(x,0,y,\xi)-1)\sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t\sigma(y,\xi)))\in S^{d-1}\] one can remove $q$ from the main term, which results in the following. \begin{lemma} There is an open set $V\subset U$ containing $0$ such that, as $L\rightarrow\infty$ and uniformly for $(x,y)\in V\times V$, \[ S_d(x,y,L)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L} \sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t\sigma(y,\xi))) e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi + O(L^{n+d-1})\,. \] \end{lemma} The juxtaposition of these results yields Lemma \ref{hol0}. \begin{prf}[ of Lemma \ref{hol1}] Since $k\in C^\infty(U\times U\times]-\varepsilon,\varepsilon[)$ and $\mathcal{F}(\rho)$ is supported in $]-\varepsilon,\varepsilon[$, \[ \mathcal{F}^{-1}_t\big[\mathcal{F}(\rho)(t)Pk(x,t,y)\big](L)\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})\, . \] Therefore, by Equation \eqref{e.ap}, \[ \rho*\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)-\int_{-\infty}^L\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\mathcal{F}^{-1}_t\Big[\mathcal{F}(\rho)P\left(q(x,t,y,\xi)e^{i(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t \sigma(y,\xi))}\right)\Big](\lambda)d\xi d\lambda \] is bounded. \end{prf} \begin{prf}[ of Lemma \ref{hol3}] In this proof, all generic constants will be implicitly uniform with respect to $(x,y)\in V\times V$. Let us fix $y\in V$ and define the following three domains of integration. \begin{align*} D_1&=\{(\lambda,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}^n\ |\ \lambda\leq L,\ \sigma(y,\xi)\leq L\}\\ D_2&=\{(\lambda,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}^n\ |\ \lambda\leq L,\ \sigma(y,\xi)>L\}\\ D_3&=\{(\lambda,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}^n\ |\ \lambda>L,\ \sigma(y,\xi)\leq L\}\, . \end{align*} Moreover, for $l=1,2,3$, let $I_l=\int_{D_l}R_j(x,y,\lambda-\sigma(y,\xi),\xi)e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi d\lambda$. We will prove that $I_2$ and $I_3$ are $O(L^{n+j-1})$. The following calculation will then yield the desired identity. Here we use Fubini's theorem and the fact that $\mathcal{F}(\rho)(0)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\rho(\lambda)d\lambda=1$. \begin{align*} S_j(x,y,L)&= I_1+I_2= I_1+I_3+O(L^{n+j-1})\\ &= \int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L}\Big[\int_{\mathbb{R}}R_j(x,y,s,\xi)ds\Big]e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi+O(L^{n+j-1})\\ &= \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L}\sigma_j(x,0,y,\xi)e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi+O(L^{n+j-1}). \end{align*} First of all, $R_j$ is rapidly decreasing in the third variable and, since $\sigma$ is elliptic of degree $1$, bounded by $\sigma(y,\xi)^j$ with respect to the last variable, $\xi$. Therefore, for each $N>0$ there is a constant $C>0$ such that \[|R_j(x,y,\lambda,\xi)|\leq \frac{C \sigma(y,\xi)^j}{(1+|\lambda|)^N}\,.\] Since $\sigma$ is elliptic of order $1$, the hypersurface $L^{-1}\{\sigma(y,\xi)=L\}\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ converges smoothly for $L\rightarrow\infty$ uniformly in $y$ to $S^*_y=\{\sigma_A(y,\xi)=1\}$ and the volume of $\{\sigma(x,\xi)= \beta\}\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is $O(\beta^{n-1})$. Taking $N= 2n+j+1$, we deduce that \begin{align*} |I_2|&\leq C\int_{-\infty}^L\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)>L}\frac{\sigma(y,\xi)^j}{(1+|\lambda-\sigma(y,\xi)|)^{2n+j+1}}d\xi d\lambda\leq C\int_{-\infty}^L\int_L^{+\infty}\frac{\beta^{n+j-1}}{(1+|\lambda-\beta|)^{2n+j+1}}d\beta d\lambda\\ &\leq C\int_L^{+\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{L-\beta}\frac{\beta^{n+j-1}}{(1+|s|)^{2n+j+1}}dsd\beta\leq C\int_L^\infty \frac{\beta^{n+j-1}}{(1+\beta-L)^{2n+j}}d\beta\\ &\leq C\int_0^{+\infty} \frac{(\gamma+L)^{n+j-1}}{(1+\gamma)^{2n+j}}d\gamma\leq C L^{n+j-1}. \end{align*} Here we applied first the change of variables $s=\lambda-\beta$ and then $\gamma=\beta-L$. The case of $I_3$ is analogous and by a similar calculation we deduce that $I_1$ is well defined. \end{prf}

nodes.name: A.3 Comparison with the convolution
nodes.statement_short: $\rho*\tilde E_{L,P}-\tilde E_{L,P}=O(L^{n+d-1})$ (Lemma A.7 via A.8, A.9).
nodes.statement: In this section we set about proving that $\tilde{E}_{L,P}$ is close enough to its convolution with $\rho$. This is encapsulated in the following lemma. \begin{lemma} There is an open set $V\subset U$ containing $0$ such that, as $L\rightarrow\infty$ and uniformly for $(x,y)\in V\times V$, \[\rho*\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)=O(L^{n+d-1})\,.\] \end{lemma} As before, the proofs are relegated to the end of the section. In order to prove Lemma \ref{hol6} we first estimate the growth of the $R_j$ as follows. \begin{lemma} There is an open set $V\subset U$ containing $0$ such that, as $L\rightarrow\infty$ and uniformly for $(x,y)\in V\times V$, \[\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} R_j(x,y,L-\sigma(y,\xi),\xi)e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi=O(L^{n+j-1})\,.\] \end{lemma} This lemma follows from a computation analogous to the bound on $I_2$ and $I_3$ given in the proof of Lemma \ref{hol3} above and the details are left to the reader. It allows us to prove a second intermediate result from which we obtain Lemma \ref{hol6} directly. \begin{lemma} There is an open set $V\subset U$ containing $0$ such that, as $L\rightarrow\infty$ and uniformly for $(x,y)\in V\times V$, \[\tilde{E}_{L+1,P}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)=O(L^{n+d-1})\,.\] \end{lemma} \begin{prf}[ of Lemma \ref{hol5}] We begin with the case where $x=y$ and $P$ is of the form $P_1\otimes P_1$. For brevity we define \[u(L)=\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,x)=\sum_{\lambda_k\leq L}|(P_1 e_k)(x)|^2\,.\] Recall $\rho>0$ so it stays greater than some constant $a>0$ on the interval $[-1,0]$. Moreover $u$ is increasing so by Equation \eqref{e.ap} and Lemma \ref{hol2}, \begin{align*} 0&\leq u(L+1)-u(L)=\int_L^{L+1}u'(\lambda)d\lambda\leq \frac{1}{a}\int_L^{L+1}\rho(L-\lambda)u'(\lambda)d\lambda\\ &\leq \frac{1}{a}\frac{d}{dL}(\rho*u)\leq \frac{1}{a}\sum_{j=0}^d \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} R_j(x,y,L-\sigma(y,\xi))d\xi +O(L^{n+d-1})=O(L^{n+d-1}). \end{align*} Now if $P$ is of the form $P_1\otimes P_2$, and for any $x$ and $y$, let $X=(P_1 e_k)_{L<\lambda_k\leq L+1}$ and $Y=(P_2 e_k)_{L<\lambda_k\leq L+1}$ be two vectors in some $\mathbb{C}^q$ which we equip with the standard hermitian product ``$\star$''. Then, $\tilde{E}_{L+1,P}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)=X\star \overline{Y}$ so \begin{align*} |\tilde{E}_{L+1,P}&(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)|^2\leq |X|^2|Y|^2\\ &=|\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_1\otimes P_1}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_1\otimes P_1}(x,y)||\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_2\otimes P_2}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_2\otimes P_2}(x,y)|\\ &\leq \frac{1}{4}\left(\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_1\otimes P_1}(x,x)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_1\otimes P_1}(x,x)+\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_1\otimes P_1}(y,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_1\otimes P_1}(y,y)\right)\\ &\times\left(\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_2\otimes P_2}(x,x)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_2\otimes P_2}(x,x)+\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_2\otimes P_2}(y,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_2\otimes P_2}(y,y)\right)\\ &\leq C L^{2n+2d-2}. \end{align*} Here we used first the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, then the mean value inequality, then on each factor, \[2|P_1 e_k(x)\overline{P_1 e_k(y)}|\leq |P_1 e_k(x)|^2+|P_1 e_k(y)|^2\] and finally the above estimate. In general $P$ is a locally finite sum of operators of the form $P_1\otimes P_2$. \end{prf} \begin{prf}[ of Lemma \ref{hol6}] First of all, according to Lemma \ref{hol5} there is a constant $C$ such that for all $L\geq 0$ and $\lambda$, \begin{equation*} |\tilde{E}_{L+\lambda,P}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)|\leq C(1+|\lambda|+L)^{n+d-1}(1+|\lambda|). \end{equation*} Consequently \begin{align*} (\rho*\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)|&\leq|\int\rho(\lambda)\tilde{E}_{L+\lambda,P}(x,y)d\lambda-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)|\\ &\leq\int\rho(\lambda)\Big|\tilde{E}_{L+\lambda,P}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)\Big|d\lambda\\ &\leq C\int\rho(\lambda)(1+|\lambda|+L)^{n+d-1}(1+|\lambda|)d\lambda\\ &\leq C'L^{n+d-1} \end{align*} for some $C'>0$. Here we used that $\rho>0$, $\rho$ is rapidly decreasing and $\int_{\mathbb{R}}\rho(\lambda)d\lambda=\mathcal{F}(\rho)(0)=1$. \end{prf}

nodes.name: A.4 Conclusion
nodes.statement_short: Combine, replace $\sigma$ by $\sigma_A^{1/m}$ and rescale $L\mapsto L^{1/m}$.
nodes.statement: Combining Lemmas \ref{hol0} and \ref{hol6} we obtain the following: \[ \tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L} \sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}\psi(x,y,\xi)) e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi + O(L^{n+d-1})\, . \] Since $\sigma-\sigma_A^{\frac{1}{m}}\in S^0$, replacing one by the other adds only a $O(L^{n+d-1})$ term. Therefore, \[ \tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma_A(y,\xi)^{1/m}\leq L} \sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}\psi(x,y,\xi)) e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi + O(L^{n+d-1})\, . \] This estimate is valid and uniform for $x,y\in V$. To conclude, notice that $\sigma_A(x,\xi)^{1/m}\leq L$ is equivalent to $\sigma_A(x,\xi)\leq L^m$. Since $\tilde{E}_L=E_{L^m}$, replacing $L$ by $L^{1/m}$ in the last estimate we get \[ E_{L,P}(x,y)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma_A(y,\xi) \leq L} \sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}\psi(x,y,\xi)) e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi + O(L^{(n+d-1)/m}) \] as announced.

nodes.name: Combine Lemmas A.3 and A.7
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotic for $\tilde E_{L,P}$.
nodes.statement: Combining Lemmas \ref{hol0} and \ref{hol6} we obtain the following: \[ \tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L} \sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}\psi(x,y,\xi)) e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi + O(L^{n+d-1})\, . \]

nodes.name: Replace sigma by sigma_A^{1/m}
nodes.statement_short: Costs $O(L^{n+d-1})$.
nodes.statement: Since $\sigma-\sigma_A^{\frac{1}{m}}\in S^0$, replacing one by the other adds only a $O(L^{n+d-1})$ term. Therefore, \[ \tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma_A(y,\xi)^{1/m}\leq L} \sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}\psi(x,y,\xi)) e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi + O(L^{n+d-1})\, . \]

nodes.name: Rescale L
nodes.statement_short: Replace $L$ by $L^{1/m}$.
nodes.statement: This estimate is valid and uniform for $x,y\in V$. To conclude, notice that $\sigma_A(x,\xi)^{1/m}\leq L$ is equivalent to $\sigma_A(x,\xi)\leq L^m$. Since $\tilde{E}_L=E_{L^m}$, replacing $L$ by $L^{1/m}$ in the last estimate we get \[ E_{L,P}(x,y)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma_A(y,\xi) \leq L} \sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}\psi(x,y,\xi)) e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi + O(L^{(n+d-1)/m}) \] as announced.

nodes.name: Rescaled spectral function tilde E_L
nodes.statement: For each $L>0$, set $\tilde{E}_L=E_{L^m}$.

nodes.name: Fourier integral parametrix for the wave kernel
nodes.statement_short: The Fourier transform in $L$ of $\tilde E_L'$ is locally a Fourier integral $\int q\,e^{i(\psi-t\sigma)}d\xi$ plus a smooth term, with $\psi$ a proper phase solving the eikonal equation.
assumptions: for each set of local coordinates in which $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$ coincides with the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$
conclusions: the spectral function $\tilde{E}_L(x,y)$ defines a tempered distribution of the $L$ variable with values in $C^\infty(\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{X})$
nodes.statement: Firstly, the spectral function $\tilde{E}_L(x,y)$ defines a tempered distribution of the $L$ variable with values in $C^\infty(\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{X})$. In addition, for each set of local coordinates in which $d\mu_{\mathcal{X}}$ coincides with the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $0\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that there exist $\varepsilon>0$, a proper phase function $\psi \in C^\infty(U\times U\times\mathbb{R}^n)$, a symbol $\sigma\in S^1(U,\mathbb{R}^n)$, a function $k\in C^\infty(U\times U\times]-\varepsilon,\varepsilon[)$ and a symbol $q\in S^0(U\times ]-\varepsilon,\varepsilon[\times U,\mathbb{R}^n)$, for which \[\mathcal{F}_L[\tilde{E}_L'(x,y)](t)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}q(x,t,y,\xi)e^{i(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t\sigma(y,\xi))}d\xi + k(x,y,t).\] Here $\mathcal{F}_L$ (resp. $'$) denotes the Fourier transform (resp. the derivative) with respect to the variable $L$, in the sense of temperate distributions, and the integral is to be understood in the sense of Fourier integral operators (see Theorem 2.4 of \cite{ho68}). We have \begin{enumerate} \item The function $\psi$ satisfies the Equation \[\forall x,y\in U,\ \xi\in \mathbb{R}^n,\ \sigma(x,\partial_x\psi(x,y,\xi))=\sigma(y,\xi).\] \item For each $t\in]-\varepsilon,\varepsilon[$ and $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n$, the function $q(\cdot,t,\cdot,\xi)$ has compact support in $U\times U$ uniformly in $(t,\xi)$ and $q(x,0,y,\xi)-1$ is a symbol of order $-1$ as long as $x,y$ belong to some open neighborhood $U_0$ of $0$ in $U$. \item $\sigma-\sigma_A^{\frac{1}{m}}\in S^0$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: l.source

nodes.name: Positive Schwartz bump with compactly supported Fourier transform
conclusions: there is a function $\rho\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$ such that $\mathcal{F}(\rho)$ has compact support contained in $]-\varepsilon,\varepsilon[$, $\rho>0$ and $\mathcal{F}(\rho)(0)=1$
nodes.statement: For each $\varepsilon>0$ there is a function $\rho\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$ such that $\mathcal{F}(\rho)$ has compact support contained in $]-\varepsilon,\varepsilon[$, $\rho>0$ and $\mathcal{F}(\rho)(0)=1$.
nodes.label: bump

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.2
nodes.statement_short: Take $\rho=f^2*f^2$ for $f$ Schwartz with Fourier support in $]-\varepsilon/2,\varepsilon/2[$.
nodes.statement: Choose $f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$ whose Fourier transform has support in $]-\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\varepsilon}{2}[$. Then it is easy to see that $\rho=f^2*f^2$ satisfies the required properties.

nodes.name: Differentiated spectral function
nodes.statement: Let $\tilde{E}_{L,P}=P\tilde{E}_L$.

nodes.name: Convolution rho * tilde E_{L,P}
nodes.statement: Then, we will compare $\tilde{E}_{L,P}$ to its convolution with $\rho$ which we denote - somewhat liberally - by \[ \rho*\tilde{E}_{L,P}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\rho(\lambda)\tilde{E}_{L-\lambda,P}d\lambda\, . \]

nodes.name: Derivative of the convolved kernel via the parametrix
nodes.statement: \frac{d}{d\lambda}(\rho*e_{\lambda,P}(x,y))|_{\lambda=L}=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\mathcal{F}^{-1}_t\Big[\mathcal{F}(\rho)(t)&P \left(q(x,t,y,\xi)e^{i(\psi(x,t,y,\xi)-t\sigma(y,\xi))}\right) \Big](L)d\xi\\\nonumber &+\mathcal{F}^{-1}_t\big[\mathcal{F}(\rho)(t)Pk(x,t,y)\big](L).
nodes.label: e.ap

nodes.name: Asymptotic of the convolved kernel
conclusions: There is an open set $V\subset U$ containing $0$ such that, as $L\rightarrow\infty$ and uniformly for $(x,y)\in V\times V$,
nodes.statement: There is an open set $V\subset U$ containing $0$ such that, as $L\rightarrow\infty$ and uniformly for $(x,y)\in V\times V$, \[\rho*\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L} \sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}\psi(x,y,\xi)) e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi + O(L^{n+d-1})\,.\]
nodes.label: hol0

nodes.name: Convolved kernel equals parametrix integral up to bounded error
conclusions: is bounded uniformly for $(x,y)\in U\times U$
nodes.statement: The quantity \[\rho*\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)-\int_{-\infty}^L\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{T^*_yM} \mathcal{F}^{-1}_t\Big[\mathcal{F}(\rho)P\left(q(x,t,y,\xi)e^{i(\psi(x,y,t,\xi)-t \sigma(y,\xi))}\right)\Big](\lambda)d\xi d\lambda\] is bounded uniformly for $(x,y)\in U\times U$.
nodes.label: hol1

nodes.name: Leibniz expansion of P applied to the parametrix
nodes.statement_short: $P(qe^{i(\psi-t\sigma)})=\sum_{j\le d}\sigma_je^{i(\psi-t\sigma)}$ with $\sigma_j$ homogeneous of degree $j$ and top term $q\sigma_P(\partial_{x,y}(\psi-t\sigma))$.
conclusions: there is a finite family of symbols $(\sigma_j)_{0\leq j\leq d}
nodes.statement: By the Leibniz rule, there is a finite family of symbols $(\sigma_j)_{0\leq j\leq d}\in C^{\infty}(U\times]-\varepsilon,\varepsilon[\times U,\mathbb{R}^n)^{d+1}$ such that for each $j$, $\sigma_j$ is homogeneous of degree $j$, such that \[P\Big[q(x,t,y,\xi)e^{i(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t\sigma(y,\xi))}\Big]=\Big[\sum_{j=0}^{d} \sigma_j(x,t,y,\xi)\Big]e^{i(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t\sigma(y,\xi))}\] and such that \[\sigma_d(x,t,y,\xi)=q(x,t,y,\xi)\sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t\sigma(y,\xi)))\,.\]

nodes.name: Auxiliary kernels R_j and S_j
nodes.statement: Now, for each $j$, let \[R_j(x,y,L,\xi)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n+1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathcal{F}(\rho)(t)\sigma_j(x,t,y,\xi)e^{itL}dt\] and \[S_j(x,y,L)=\int_{-\infty}^L\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} R_j(x,y,\lambda-\sigma(y,\xi),\xi)e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi d\lambda\,.\]

nodes.name: Growth of S_j
conclusions: There is an open set $V\subset U$ containing $0$ such that, as $L\rightarrow\infty$ and uniformly for $(x,y)\in V\times V$,
nodes.statement: There is an open set $V\subset U$ containing $0$ such that, as $L\rightarrow\infty$ and uniformly for $(x,y)\in V\times V$, \[S_j(x,y,L)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L}\sigma_j(x,0,y,\xi)e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi+O(L^{n+j-1})\,.\]
nodes.label: hol3

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.6
nodes.statement_short: Same computation as Lemma A.5 with the lower-order symbol (q-1)sigma_P, left to the reader.
nodes.statement: Similarly since $q(x,0,y,\xi)-1\in S^{-1}(U_0\times U_0,\mathbb{R}^n)$, from a computation analogous to the proof of Lemma \ref{hol3} and left to the reader, replacing $\sigma_d$ by \[(q(x,0,y,\xi)-1)\sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t\sigma(y,\xi)))\in S^{d-1}\] one can remove $q$ from the main term, which results in the following.

nodes.name: Removing q from the main term
conclusions: There is an open set $V\subset U$ containing $0$ such that, as $L\rightarrow\infty$ and uniformly for $(x,y)\in V\times V$,
nodes.statement: There is an open set $V\subset U$ containing $0$ such that, as $L\rightarrow\infty$ and uniformly for $(x,y)\in V\times V$, \[ S_d(x,y,L)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L} \sigma_P(x,y,\partial_{x,y}(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t\sigma(y,\xi))) e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi + O(L^{n+d-1})\,. \]
nodes.label: hol4

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.3
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemmas A.4, A.5 and A.6.
nodes.statement: The juxtaposition of these results yields Lemma \ref{hol0}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.4
nodes.statement_short: The smooth remainder $k$ contributes a Schwartz function, hence a bounded term.
nodes.statement: Since $k\in C^\infty(U\times U\times]-\varepsilon,\varepsilon[)$ and $\mathcal{F}(\rho)$ is supported in $]-\varepsilon,\varepsilon[$, \[ \mathcal{F}^{-1}_t\big[\mathcal{F}(\rho)(t)Pk(x,t,y)\big](L)\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})\, . \] Therefore, by Equation \eqref{e.ap}, \[ \rho*\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)-\int_{-\infty}^L\frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\mathcal{F}^{-1}_t\Big[\mathcal{F}(\rho)P\left(q(x,t,y,\xi)e^{i(\psi(x,y,\xi)-t \sigma(y,\xi))}\right)\Big](\lambda)d\xi d\lambda \] is bounded.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.5
nodes.statement_short: Split the $(\lambda,\xi)$ domain into three regions; the off-diagonal regions are $O(L^{n+j-1})$ by rapid decay of $R_j$, and Fubini on the main region gives the integral of $\sigma_j(x,0,y,\xi)$.
nodes.statement: In this proof, all generic constants will be implicitly uniform with respect to $(x,y)\in V\times V$. Let us fix $y\in V$ and define the following three domains of integration. \begin{align*} D_1&=\{(\lambda,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}^n\ |\ \lambda\leq L,\ \sigma(y,\xi)\leq L\}\\ D_2&=\{(\lambda,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}^n\ |\ \lambda\leq L,\ \sigma(y,\xi)>L\}\\ D_3&=\{(\lambda,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}^n\ |\ \lambda>L,\ \sigma(y,\xi)\leq L\}\, . \end{align*} Moreover, for $l=1,2,3$, let $I_l=\int_{D_l}R_j(x,y,\lambda-\sigma(y,\xi),\xi)e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi d\lambda$. We will prove that $I_2$ and $I_3$ are $O(L^{n+j-1})$. The following calculation will then yield the desired identity. Here we use Fubini's theorem and the fact that $\mathcal{F}(\rho)(0)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\rho(\lambda)d\lambda=1$. \begin{align*} S_j(x,y,L)&= I_1+I_2= I_1+I_3+O(L^{n+j-1})\\ &= \int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L}\Big[\int_{\mathbb{R}}R_j(x,y,s,\xi)ds\Big]e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi+O(L^{n+j-1})\\ &= \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L}\sigma_j(x,0,y,\xi)e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi+O(L^{n+j-1}). \end{align*} First of all, $R_j$ is rapidly decreasing in the third variable and, since $\sigma$ is elliptic of degree $1$, bounded by $\sigma(y,\xi)^j$ with respect to the last variable, $\xi$. Therefore, for each $N>0$ there is a constant $C>0$ such that \[|R_j(x,y,\lambda,\xi)|\leq \frac{C \sigma(y,\xi)^j}{(1+|\lambda|)^N}\,.\] Since $\sigma$ is elliptic of order $1$, the hypersurface $L^{-1}\{\sigma(y,\xi)=L\}\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ converges smoothly for $L\rightarrow\infty$ uniformly in $y$ to $S^*_y=\{\sigma_A(y,\xi)=1\}$ and the volume of $\{\sigma(x,\xi)= \beta\}\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is $O(\beta^{n-1})$. Taking $N= 2n+j+1$, we deduce that \begin{align*} |I_2|&\leq C\int_{-\infty}^L\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)>L}\frac{\sigma(y,\xi)^j}{(1+|\lambda-\sigma(y,\xi)|)^{2n+j+1}}d\xi d\lambda\leq C\int_{-\infty}^L\int_L^{+\infty}\frac{\beta^{n+j-1}}{(1+|\lambda-\beta|)^{2n+j+1}}d\beta d\lambda\\ &\leq C\int_L^{+\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{L-\beta}\frac{\beta^{n+j-1}}{(1+|s|)^{2n+j+1}}dsd\beta\leq C\int_L^\infty \frac{\beta^{n+j-1}}{(1+\beta-L)^{2n+j}}d\beta\\ &\leq C\int_0^{+\infty} \frac{(\gamma+L)^{n+j-1}}{(1+\gamma)^{2n+j}}d\gamma\leq C L^{n+j-1}. \end{align*} Here we applied first the change of variables $s=\lambda-\beta$ and then $\gamma=\beta-L$. The case of $I_3$ is analogous and by a similar calculation we deduce that $I_1$ is well defined.

nodes.name: Three domains
nodes.statement_short: Define $D_1,D_2,D_3$.
nodes.statement: In this proof, all generic constants will be implicitly uniform with respect to $(x,y)\in V\times V$. Let us fix $y\in V$ and define the following three domains of integration. \begin{align*} D_1&=\{(\lambda,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}^n\ |\ \lambda\leq L,\ \sigma(y,\xi)\leq L\}\\ D_2&=\{(\lambda,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}^n\ |\ \lambda\leq L,\ \sigma(y,\xi)>L\}\\ D_3&=\{(\lambda,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}^n\ |\ \lambda>L,\ \sigma(y,\xi)\leq L\}\, . \end{align*}

nodes.name: Reduction to I_2, I_3
nodes.statement_short: It suffices that $I_2,I_3=O(L^{n+j-1})$; Fubini gives the main term.
nodes.statement: Moreover, for $l=1,2,3$, let $I_l=\int_{D_l}R_j(x,y,\lambda-\sigma(y,\xi),\xi)e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi d\lambda$. We will prove that $I_2$ and $I_3$ are $O(L^{n+j-1})$. The following calculation will then yield the desired identity. Here we use Fubini's theorem and the fact that $\mathcal{F}(\rho)(0)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\rho(\lambda)d\lambda=1$. \begin{align*} S_j(x,y,L)&= I_1+I_2= I_1+I_3+O(L^{n+j-1})\\ &= \int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L}\Big[\int_{\mathbb{R}}R_j(x,y,s,\xi)ds\Big]e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi+O(L^{n+j-1})\\ &= \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)\leq L}\sigma_j(x,0,y,\xi)e^{i\psi(x,y,\xi)}d\xi+O(L^{n+j-1}). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Decay of R_j
nodes.statement_short: $|R_j|\le C\sigma^j(1+|\lambda|)^{-N}$.
nodes.statement: First of all, $R_j$ is rapidly decreasing in the third variable and, since $\sigma$ is elliptic of degree $1$, bounded by $\sigma(y,\xi)^j$ with respect to the last variable, $\xi$. Therefore, for each $N>0$ there is a constant $C>0$ such that \[|R_j(x,y,\lambda,\xi)|\leq \frac{C \sigma(y,\xi)^j}{(1+|\lambda|)^N}\,.\]

nodes.name: Bound I_2
nodes.statement: Since $\sigma$ is elliptic of order $1$, the hypersurface $L^{-1}\{\sigma(y,\xi)=L\}\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ converges smoothly for $L\rightarrow\infty$ uniformly in $y$ to $S^*_y=\{\sigma_A(y,\xi)=1\}$ and the volume of $\{\sigma(x,\xi)= \beta\}\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is $O(\beta^{n-1})$. Taking $N= 2n+j+1$, we deduce that \begin{align*} |I_2|&\leq C\int_{-\infty}^L\int_{\sigma(y,\xi)>L}\frac{\sigma(y,\xi)^j}{(1+|\lambda-\sigma(y,\xi)|)^{2n+j+1}}d\xi d\lambda\leq C\int_{-\infty}^L\int_L^{+\infty}\frac{\beta^{n+j-1}}{(1+|\lambda-\beta|)^{2n+j+1}}d\beta d\lambda\\ &\leq C\int_L^{+\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{L-\beta}\frac{\beta^{n+j-1}}{(1+|s|)^{2n+j+1}}dsd\beta\leq C\int_L^\infty \frac{\beta^{n+j-1}}{(1+\beta-L)^{2n+j}}d\beta\\ &\leq C\int_0^{+\infty} \frac{(\gamma+L)^{n+j-1}}{(1+\gamma)^{2n+j}}d\gamma\leq C L^{n+j-1}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: I_3 analogous
nodes.statement_short: Same for $I_3$.
nodes.statement: Here we applied first the change of variables $s=\lambda-\beta$ and then $\gamma=\beta-L$. The case of $I_3$ is analogous and by a similar calculation we deduce that $I_1$ is well defined.

nodes.statement_short: Analogous to the bound on I_2, I_3 in Lemma A.5; left to the reader.

nodes.name: Unit increments of the spectral function
conclusions: \tilde{E}_{L+1,P}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)=O(L^{n+d-1})

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.9
nodes.statement_short: On the diagonal with $P=P_1\otimes P_1$, monotonicity and positivity of $\rho$ bound unit increments by the derivative of the convolution; general $P$ by Cauchy-Schwarz.
nodes.section: A.3 Comparison of the kernel and its convolution
nodes.statement: We begin with the case where $x=y$ and $P$ is of the form $P_1\otimes P_1$. For brevity we define \[u(L)=\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,x)=\sum_{\lambda_k\leq L}|(P_1 e_k)(x)|^2\,.\] Recall $\rho>0$ so it stays greater than some constant $a>0$ on the interval $[-1,0]$. Moreover $u$ is increasing so by Equation \eqref{e.ap} and Lemma \ref{hol2}, \begin{align*} 0&\leq u(L+1)-u(L)=\int_L^{L+1}u'(\lambda)d\lambda\leq \frac{1}{a}\int_L^{L+1}\rho(L-\lambda)u'(\lambda)d\lambda\\ &\leq \frac{1}{a}\frac{d}{dL}(\rho*u)\leq \frac{1}{a}\sum_{j=0}^d \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} R_j(x,y,L-\sigma(y,\xi))d\xi +O(L^{n+d-1})=O(L^{n+d-1}). \end{align*} Now if $P$ is of the form $P_1\otimes P_2$, and for any $x$ and $y$, let $X=(P_1 e_k)_{L<\lambda_k\leq L+1}$ and $Y=(P_2 e_k)_{L<\lambda_k\leq L+1}$ be two vectors in some $\mathbb{C}^q$ which we equip with the standard hermitian product ``$\star$''. Then, $\tilde{E}_{L+1,P}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)=X\star \overline{Y}$ so \begin{align*} |\tilde{E}_{L+1,P}&(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)|^2\leq |X|^2|Y|^2\\ &=|\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_1\otimes P_1}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_1\otimes P_1}(x,y)||\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_2\otimes P_2}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_2\otimes P_2}(x,y)|\\ &\leq \frac{1}{4}\left(\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_1\otimes P_1}(x,x)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_1\otimes P_1}(x,x)+\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_1\otimes P_1}(y,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_1\otimes P_1}(y,y)\right)\\ &\times\left(\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_2\otimes P_2}(x,x)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_2\otimes P_2}(x,x)+\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_2\otimes P_2}(y,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_2\otimes P_2}(y,y)\right)\\ &\leq C L^{2n+2d-2}. \end{align*} Here we used first the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, then the mean value inequality, then on each factor, \[2|P_1 e_k(x)\overline{P_1 e_k(y)}|\leq |P_1 e_k(x)|^2+|P_1 e_k(y)|^2\] and finally the above estimate. In general $P$ is a locally finite sum of operators of the form $P_1\otimes P_2$.

Then, $\tilde{E}_{L+1,P}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)=X\star \overline{Y}$ so \begin{align*} |\tilde{E}_{L+1,P}&(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)|^2\leq |X|^2|Y|^2\\ &=|\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_1\otimes P_1}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_1\otimes P_1}(x,y)||\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_2\otimes P_2}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_2\otimes P_2}(x,y)|\\ &\leq \frac{1}{4}\left(\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_1\otimes P_1}(x,x)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_1\otimes P_1}(x,x)+\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_1\otimes P_1}(y,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_1\otimes P_1}(y,y)\right)\\ &\times\left(\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_2\otimes P_2}(x,x)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_2\otimes P_2}(x,x)+\tilde{E}_{L+1,P_2\otimes P_2}(y,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P_2\otimes P_2}(y,y)\right)\\ &\leq C L^{2n+2d-2}. \end{align*}

nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz, AM-GM and the diagonal estimate.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.7
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the increment bound of Lemma A.9 against $\rho$, using its rapid decay and unit mass.
nodes.section: A.3 Comparison of the kernel and its convolution
nodes.statement: First of all, according to Lemma \ref{hol5} there is a constant $C$ such that for all $L\geq 0$ and $\lambda$, \begin{equation*} |\tilde{E}_{L+\lambda,P}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)|\leq C(1+|\lambda|+L)^{n+d-1}(1+|\lambda|). \end{equation*} Consequently \begin{align*} (\rho*\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)|&\leq|\int\rho(\lambda)\tilde{E}_{L+\lambda,P}(x,y)d\lambda-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)|\\ &\leq\int\rho(\lambda)\Big|\tilde{E}_{L+\lambda,P}(x,y)-\tilde{E}_{L,P}(x,y)\Big|d\lambda\\ &\leq C\int\rho(\lambda)(1+|\lambda|+L)^{n+d-1}(1+|\lambda|)d\lambda\\ &\leq C'L^{n+d-1} \end{align*} for some $C'>0$. Here we used that $\rho>0$, $\rho$ is rapidly decreasing and $\int_{\mathbb{R}}\rho(\lambda)d\lambda=\mathcal{F}(\rho)(0)=1$.
